title: Types of Vectors
notes: **Like (parallel) vectors**: vectors having the same direction, regardless of their magnitudes. They can be written as $\vec{A} = a\vec{B}$ where $a$ is a positive scalar. Like vectors add by ordinary arithmetic: their resultant is also parallel to them.

**Unlike (anti-parallel) vectors**: vectors having exactly opposite directions. If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are anti-parallel, $\vec{A} = -a\vec{B}$ where $a$ is a positive scalar. The dot product of two anti-parallel vectors is $-|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|$.

**Co-planar vectors**: vectors that lie in the same plane. Any two vectors are always coplanar. Three vectors are coplanar if their vector sum or the scalar triple product $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 0$.

**Non-coplanar (skew) vectors**: vectors that do not lie in the same plane. Three vectors are non-coplanar if they span 3D space. The minimum number of non-coplanar vectors needed to span 3D is three.

**Null (zero) vector $\vec{0}$**: a vector with zero magnitude and indeterminate direction. It is the additive identity: $\vec{A} + \vec{0} = \vec{A}$. The zero vector is parallel to every vector, since $0\vec{A} = \vec{0}$.

**Unit vector**: a vector of magnitude 1 in a specified direction, denoted with a hat/circumflex: $\hat{n}$, $\hat{A}$. For any vector $\vec{A}$, the unit vector along it is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.

**Standard unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$**: unit vectors along the x, y, and z axes of a Cartesian coordinate system. They are mutually perpendicular: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{i} = 0$ and $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$ (right-hand rule).

**Position vector**: the vector from the origin to a point, denoted $\vec{r}$. If the point is $(x, y, z)$, then $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$. It specifies the location of a point relative to the origin.

**Equal vectors**: two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude AND the same direction. They can be drawn from different points but are physically equivalent: $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$ implies $|\vec{A}| = |\vec{B}|$ and parallel with same orientation.

**Negative vector**: $-\vec{A}$ is the vector with the same magnitude as $\vec{A}$ but opposite direction. $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$. Useful in problems like relative velocity and force balance.
**Collinear vectors**: vectors lying along the same line, regardless of direction. They are either parallel or anti-parallel. Collinear vectors add algebraically with appropriate signs.

**Axial vector (pseudovector)**: vectors representing quantities like angular velocity, torque, and magnetic field. They change sign under reflection (mirror inversion). In contrast, **polar vectors** (force, velocity) follow normal vector addition.

**Free vector**: a vector that can be translated parallel to itself without changing its physical meaning. Examples: velocity, force. In contrast, a **bound (localized) vector** is tied to a specific point (e.g., moment of a force about a point).

**Basis vectors**: a set of linearly independent vectors that span the entire vector space. For 3D, $\{\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\}$ is the standard basis. Any vector in 3D can be written as a linear combination of basis vectors.
**Orthogonal vectors**: vectors that are perpendicular to each other. The dot product of orthogonal vectors is zero: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$ for perpendicular $\vec{A}, \vec{B}$.

**Mutually perpendicular vectors**: a set of vectors where each is perpendicular to every other. $\{\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\}$ is the canonical example in 3D. The magnitude of any vector is the square root of the sum of squares of components along such a basis.

**Solved example**: two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$. But 'parallel' only requires same direction, allowing different magnitudes. So parallel does not imply equal, but equal implies parallel.

**Collinear three-vector property**: if $\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}$ are collinear, then $\vec{C} = a\vec{A} + b\vec{B}$ for some scalars $a, b$ (and conversely, three collinear vectors are linearly dependent).

**Vector notation distinction**: bold $\mathbf{A}$ and arrow $\vec{A}$ both denote vectors. Magnitude is $|\vec{A}|$, $|\mathbf{A}|$, or simply $A$. Unit vectors are $\hat{a}$ or $\hat{u}$ (with hat).

**Practical applications**: in physics, identifying the type of vector helps in selecting the correct operation. Force is a polar vector (adds via parallelogram law), torque is an axial vector (different rules for reflection).

**Contravariant vs covariant vectors**: in advanced vector analysis, vectors are classified by how their components transform under coordinate changes. Contravariant components transform opposite to basis vectors; covariant components transform the same way. This distinction is crucial in tensor analysis and general relativity.

**Basis-independent definition**: a vector is fundamentally defined as an object that transforms in a specific way under coordinate rotations. The component representation $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$ is basis-dependent, but the vector itself is a geometric object independent of coordinates.

**Linear dependence and independence**: a set of vectors is linearly independent if no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. In 3D, at most 3 vectors can be linearly independent. Four or more vectors in 3D are always linearly dependent.

**Zero vector and linear dependence**: the zero vector is always linearly dependent with any set of vectors (since $0\cdot\vec{A} + 0\cdot\vec{B} + 1\cdot\vec{0} = \vec{0}$). Any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

**Coplanarity test for three vectors**: three vectors $\vec{A}$, $\vec{B}$, $\vec{C}$ are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product is zero: $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 0$. This is equivalent to the volume of the parallelepiped they form being zero.
confusion: Like vectors are equal — Like vectors are parallel (same direction), but their magnitudes can differ. Equal vectors require both same direction and same magnitude. $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B} = 5\hat{i}$ are like vectors but not equal.
The null vector has no direction at all — The null vector has indeterminate direction, meaning we cannot assign a unique direction to it. By convention, it is treated as parallel to every vector.

All vectors in 3D are coplanar — Any TWO vectors are coplanar, but three vectors can be non-coplanar (skew). Four or more vectors can always be reduced to a set in 3D, with at most 3 linearly independent members.

Unit vectors are unique for each direction — There are infinitely many unit vectors for the same direction (any vector of magnitude 1 in that direction). However, for a given direction, the unit vector is unique up to sign.

Co-planar and parallel mean the same thing — Parallel vectors must lie along the same line (collinear). Coplanar vectors only need to be in the same plane; they can point in different directions within that plane.
Anti-parallel vectors are like vectors with a sign — Anti-parallel vectors point in OPPOSITE directions. Like vectors point in the SAME direction. They are fundamentally different categories.

Equal vectors must start at the same point — No. Free vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of position. The position of the vector's tail or head does not affect its equality.

Position vector and displacement vector are the same — Position vector $\vec{r}$ is from origin to a point. Displacement vector $\Delta\vec{r}$ is the change in position from one point to another. They are related but not identical.
The negative of a vector changes its magnitude — No. The negative vector $-\vec{A}$ has the SAME magnitude as $\vec{A}$ but the OPPOSITE direction. Only the direction changes.

All unit vectors are the same — No. Each unit vector points in a different direction. $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$ are all unit vectors but point in different (mutually perpendicular) directions. There are infinitely many unit vectors, one for each direction.
practice: State which of the following pairs of vectors are like, unlike, coplanar, or equal: (a) $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i}$, $\vec{B} = 7\hat{i}$. (b) $\vec{A} = 4\hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = -6\hat{j}$. (c) $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$. [Solution: (a) like, coplanar, not equal (different magnitudes). (b) unlike, coplanar, not equal. (c) equal (and therefore like, coplanar, parallel).]

Are the vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{C} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$ coplanar? [Solution: Compute the scalar triple product $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C})$. First, $\vec{B}\times\vec{C} = \hat{i}((-2)(5)-(1)(1)) - \hat{j}((1)(5)-(1)(3)) + \hat{k}((1)(1)-(-2)(3)) = -11\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$. Then $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 2(-11) + 3(-2) + 4(7) = -22 - 6 + 28 = 0$. Since the scalar triple product is 0, the vectors are coplanar.]

Show that the zero vector $\vec{0}$ is parallel to every vector. [Solution: For any $\vec{A}$, the zero vector can be written as $\vec{0} = 0\cdot\vec{A}$. The scalar multiplier is 0, which is a non-negative real number. So $\vec{0}$ is parallel to $\vec{A}$ by the definition of parallelism. Also, $\vec{0}$ has no specific direction, so the convention treats it as parallel to all directions.]

If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are unit vectors making 60° with each other, find $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = \sqrt{1+1+2\cos60°} = \sqrt{2+1} = \sqrt{3}$. Direction: bisects the angle, so 30° from each. $\vec{A}+\vec{B} = \sqrt{3}\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector at 30° from both.]

Determine whether the vectors $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, $\vec{C} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ are coplanar. [Solution: $\vec{B}\times\vec{C} = \hat{i}((-3)(3)-(5)(-1)) - \hat{j}((1)(3)-(5)(2)) + \hat{k}((1)(-1)-(-3)(2)) = -4\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 3(-4) + (-2)(7) + 1(5) = -12 - 14 + 5 = -21 \neq 0$. Not coplanar.]

Express the vector $\vec{F} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$ in terms of its magnitude and a unit vector along it. [Solution: $|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{36+64} = 10$. $\hat{F} = (6/10)\hat{i} + (8/10)\hat{j} = 0.6\hat{i} + 0.8\hat{j}$. $\vec{F} = 10(0.6\hat{i}+0.8\hat{j}) = 10\hat{F}$.]

Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = -4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j}$, show that the vectors are anti-parallel. [Solution: $\vec{B} = -2(2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}) = -2\vec{A}$. The negative scalar indicates opposite direction. So $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are anti-parallel. Verify: $B/A = |-4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}|/|2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}| = \sqrt{52}/\sqrt{13} = 2$. The ratio is negative, confirming anti-parallel.]

Find three unit vectors that are mutually perpendicular to each other. [Solution: The standard unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ are mutually perpendicular: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=0$, $\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=0$, $\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}=0$. Any rotation of this set also gives three mutually perpendicular unit vectors.]

Show that the vectors $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, and $\vec{C} = \vec{B} - \vec{A} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{k}$ form a triangle. Find its type and area. [Solution: $\vec{A}+\vec{C} = \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{i}+\hat{k} = -\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} = \vec{B}$, so the triangle closes. Magnitudes: $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{2}$, $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{3}$, $|\vec{C}|=\sqrt{5}$. Check: $2+3=5$, so $|\vec{A}|^2+|\vec{B}|^2 = |\vec{C}|^2$ — it is a right-angled triangle with the right angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Verify: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -1+1+0 = 0$. Area $= \frac{1}{2}|\vec{A}||\vec{B}| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} \approx 1.225$.]

If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are unit vectors with $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 1/2$, find the angle between them and the magnitude of $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\cos\theta = \cos\theta = 1/2$, so $\theta = 60°$. $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = \sqrt{1+1+2\cos60°} = \sqrt{2+1} = \sqrt{3}$.]

Three mutually perpendicular unit vectors $\hat{u}_1$, $\hat{u}_2$, $\hat{u}_3$ form a basis for 3D space. Express an arbitrary vector $\vec{A} = 5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$ in terms of this basis. [Solution: The standard basis $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ IS a set of three mutually perpendicular unit vectors. $\vec{A}$ is already expressed in this basis: $A_x = 5$, $A_y = 12$, $A_z = 0$. The magnitude is $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{25+144} = 13$.]
universalFacts: The classification of vectors into types (like/unlike, coplanar/non-coplanar, polar/axial) is essential for choosing the right operation. Like vectors add algebraically; non-coplanar vectors require 3D analysis.
NEB exam pattern: 'types of vectors' questions are usually short answer or fill-in-the-blank format. Common question: 'define and give an example of unit vector/like vector/co-planar vector'.

The **right-hand rule** for unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ is essential for cross products: $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$. This cyclic order defines the orientation of 3D space.

**Polarity** of vectors (polar vs axial) matters in electromagnetism. Electric field $\vec{E}$ is a polar vector, magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is axial. The Lorentz force $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ produces a polar force from the cross product of two vectors of different polarities.

The **zero vector** is unique in that it is the only vector with indeterminate direction. It is the additive identity, and it is parallel to every vector (since $\vec{0} = 0 \cdot \vec{A}$ for any $\vec{A}$).

In **linear algebra**, the concept of basis vectors generalizes $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ to any set of linearly independent vectors. The 3D space we work in has dimension 3, requiring exactly 3 linearly independent basis vectors.

The **displacement vector** $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i$ is a fundamental concept in kinematics. It depends only on initial and final positions, not on the path taken — this is why the work-energy theorem works.

**Co-planar vectors** simplify problems enormously: any problem with three or more vectors that are coplanar can be analyzed in 2D using x and y components. Non-coplanar vectors require full 3D analysis.

The concept of **linear independence** is fundamental: three non-coplanar vectors form a basis for 3D space. Any vector in 3D can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of three linearly independent vectors.

**Vector spaces in physics**: the set of all displacement vectors in 3D space forms a vector space. Similarly, the set of all force vectors forms a vector space. Understanding vector types helps identify which vector space a physical quantity belongs to.
